title: From God to the Atom and Back
subtitle: A travelogue from the frontier of fundamental physics: "Looks like Ancient Greece"

blocks.html: When I was a little boy, my father (a physician) told me that reality is basically made up of little bits of stuff pushing each other around by the fundamental forces. I learned about how protons, neutrons, and electrons combine to form atoms; that the particle of light is the photon—the strange, virtually massless keeper of the cosmic speed limit. Electrons orbit atomic nuclei, atoms are bonded into crystals and molecules, and small molecules are bonded and folded into larger ones. Gravity keeps us on the ground and the Earth and Moon in their orbits. Like most kids, my exposure to this fundamental ontology was lightweight at least until high school. Atoms and molecules came up in elementary school science class; I recall a book about black holes for young readers; I enjoyed the Earth and Space museum. Through my dad and the wider culture, I had been introduced to the long tradition of materialist reductionism often identified with Democritus, whom Aristotle credited with the theory of the atom (ἄτομον).

Democritus, along with his mentor, Leucippus, developed the idea of atomism, which posited that all matter is composed of tiny, indivisible, and indestructible units called atoms (from the Greek atomos, meaning "uncuttable" or "indivisible").

Democritus theorized that atoms varied in shape, size, and motion and moved through a void, combining to form all observable phenomena. This idea was entirely philosophical, as it was based on reasoning rather than empirical evidence. When I first learned about Plato, it was not in science class. The project materials, including a technical paper and a book-length discussion, introduce a framework for a Theory of Everything—that is, a theory of fundamental physics that may be capable of “unifying” physics—called Observer Patch Holography, also the name of the project’s GitHub repository.
